meta.title: Whisper quantization WER degradation curve
meta.question: What INT quantization level produces the first statistically significant WER degradation in Whisper vs FP16 on clean speech?

pitch.one_line_answer: INT8 is near-lossless on clean speech (4.73% word error rate vs 4.94% at full precision, 47% smaller) — but so is INT4: 5.15% vs 4.94% (+4.2%, statistically not significant) and 71% smaller. The predicted degradation cliff does not exist on this corpus.
pitch.elevator: The received wisdom: quantizing Whisper below full precision hurts transcription accuracy, so pick the highest bit-width you can afford. This project measured the actual degradation curve on the LibriSpeech clean-speech corpus with a paired statistical test (Wilcoxon signed-rank) — and found no statistically significant word-error-rate penalty even at INT4. large-v3 resists quantization far better than predicted on clean speech; the size savings are real (71% at Q4_0), and the accuracy cost, on this corpus, is not measurable.

hypotheses.statement: Under LibriSpeech test-clean conditions, INT4-quantized Whisper large-v3 shows statistically significant WER degradation (p <= 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and >10% relative WER increase vs FP16 baseline.
Under LibriSpeech test-clean conditions, INT8-quantized Whisper large-v3 shows no statistically significant WER degradation vs FP16 (p > 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank), with relative WER increase < 5%.

headline.text: INT4: word error rate 5.15% vs 4.94% at full precision (+4.2% relative, p=0.57) — not statistically significant, crossing neither the 10% nor the significance thresholds
INT8: word error rate 4.73% vs 4.94% (-4.2% relative, p=0.38) — near-lossless on large-v3 clean speech
INT5: word error rate 4.64% vs 4.94% (-6.1% relative, p=0.50) — the best measured level on this corpus

journey.title: Two hypotheses, one pipeline
journey.summary: The literature gave the falsifier a shape: INT4 degradation would have to be both statistically significant and exceed 10% relative word-error-rate increase to matter; INT8 was expected to be near-lossless. Two hypotheses fixed both sides of the curve before any measurement existed.

journey.title: The pipeline was verified before it was trusted
journey.summary: The transcription-to-word-error-rate-to-statistical-test pipeline was proven end-to-end on a small model first (E-004), so a surprising result could not be blamed on broken machinery.

journey.title: The degradation cliff was not there
journey.summary: 100 random clean-speech samples, paired per-sample word error rates: INT8 at 4.73% vs 4.94% full precision (-4.2%, p=0.38); INT5 at 4.64% (-6.1%, p=0.50); INT4 at 5.15% (+4.2%, p=0.57, not significant). None of the degradation is statistically significant. The expected cliff is absent. The honest headline is 'INT8 is near-lossless', because that was the hypothesis that survived — the INT4 result is the surprise, reported as a falsification rather than spun as a win.

lessons: Clean speech is the easiest case for quantization — the result is strongest where degradation is least likely. The interesting measurement is noisy speech, and this corpus does not cover it; that gap is the most valuable next step.
Verifying the pipeline on a small model before the expensive large-v3 run separated machinery errors from surprising results — the falsified hypothesis would have been far less credible otherwise.
Writing two hypotheses — one expected to fail, one expected to hold — turned a partial result into a complete answer: both halves of the degradation curve are covered by claims made before the data.

limitations.baseline_wins: Full precision remains the reference accuracy, and no quantization level beat it with statistical significance — the measured differences (-4.2% to +4.2%) are noise-level. What changed is the knowledge of how much accuracy lower precisions give up on clean speech: a statistically undetectable amount.
limitations.untested: 100 random clean-speech samples only; the noisy-speech half of the corpus was not run. Non-English corpora untested. The sample size bounds what a statistical test can detect — a real penalty below about 4% could hide under it.
limitations.next_level: To extend the curve: run the same paired test on noisy speech, where degradation is expected to appear first, and increase the sample size for tighter confidence intervals. That is a new measurement, not more of this one.
limitations.structural: The quantization schemes tested are those of the whisper.cpp runtime (Q8_0, Q4_0), not every INT variant; results do not transfer to other runtimes. The 95% confidence interval for INT4 is [3.49%, 7.00%] — 'no degradation' holds only within that band.

audience.who_is_this_for: Engineers choosing a whisper.cpp quantization level for memory-constrained deployments on clean speech — this is the measured trade-off table between size and accuracy they currently have to guess at.
audience.not_for: Anyone deploying on noisy or multilingual audio, where these numbers do not apply — this page says so explicitly rather than letting the clean-speech result overgeneralise.
